Filipino dishes.Adobo: Adobo, braised in vinegar, soy sauce, and garlic, is often called the national dish. The vinegar acts as a preservative, handy in a tropical climate.
Filipino dishes.Sinigang: Sinigang is a sour Filipino soup, typically soured with tamarind. It is a comfort food of pork, shrimp, or fish with vegetables.
Filipino dishes.Lechon: Lechon is a whole roast pig with crackling skin, the star of Filipino feasts. Cebu's version is so well seasoned that it needs no sauce.
Filipino dishes.Lumpia: Lumpia are Filipino spring rolls from Hokkien Chinese roots. Lumpiang Shanghai, filled with ground pork, is a party favorite.
Filipino dishes.Pancit: Pancit means noodles in Filipino, and it is served at birthdays because long noodles stand for long life. The word comes from Hokkien Chinese.
Filipino dishes.Halo-halo: Halo-halo means mix-mix, a shaved ice dessert with sweet beans, jelly, fruit, and ice cream. Ube ice cream often crowns it.
Filipino dishes.Kare-kare: Kare-kare is a Filipino stew of oxtail in thick peanut sauce, tinted orange with annatto. It is eaten with salty shrimp paste.
Filipino dishes.Sisig: Sisig is chopped pork face and ears, served sizzling, and it comes from Pampanga. Chef Anthony Bourdain called it a top Filipino dish.
Filipino dishes.Turon: Turon is a Filipino snack of banana and jackfruit rolled in a wrapper, fried with caramelized sugar. It is sold by street vendors.
Filipino dishes.Bibingka: Bibingka is a rice cake cooked in clay pots with coals above and below. It is a Christmas treat sold outside churches after dawn masses.
Filipino dishes.Tocino: Tocino is sweet cured pork, bright red, eaten for breakfast with garlic rice and egg. The name comes from the Spanish word for bacon.
Filipino dishes.Rendang: Rendang is a slow-cooked, dry curry beef from the Minangkabau of Indonesia. CNN readers once ranked it among the world's best foods.
Filipino dishes.Nasi goreng: Nasi goreng is Indonesian fried rice with sweet soy sauce. It is a national dish of Indonesia, not the Philippines.
Filipino dishes.Laksa: Laksa is a spicy noodle soup from Malaysia and Singapore. Its coconut broth is distinct from Filipino dishes.
Filipino dishes.Pho: Pho is a Vietnamese beef noodle soup, not Filipino. It developed in northern Vietnam in the early 1900s.
Filipino dishes.Pad thai: Pad thai is a stir-fried Thai noodle dish. A 1930s Thai government promoted it to build national identity, so it is Thai, not Filipino.
Filipino dishes.Banh mi: Banh mi is a Vietnamese baguette sandwich, a legacy of French colonial rule. It is Vietnamese, not Filipino.
Filipino dishes.Satay: Satay is grilled skewered meat with peanut sauce, popular in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand. It's not a Filipino dish.
Filipino dishes.Bibimbap: Bibimbap is a Korean rice bowl with vegetables and egg. The name means mixed rice, and it is Korean, not Filipino.
Filipino dishes.Ramen: Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup of Chinese origin. It is not a Filipino dish.
Filipino dishes.Tom yum: Tom yum is a hot and sour Thai soup of lemongrass and galangal. It is Thai, not Filipino.
Filipino dishes.Gado-gado: Gado-gado is an Indonesian salad of vegetables with peanut sauce. The name means mix-mix in Indonesian, but it is Indonesian, not Filipino.
Filipino dishes.Massaman curry: Massaman curry is a mild, rich Thai curry with Persian-influenced spices. It is Thai, not Filipino.
Filipino dishes.Char kway teow: Char kway teow is stir-fried flat rice noodles from Malaysia and Singapore. It is not Filipino.

Drinks that contain alcohol.Sake: Rice wine, which is brewed rather than distilled, and typically about 15 percent alcohol.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Soju: A clear Korean spirit, historically from rice, and one of the best-selling spirits in the world.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Sangria: A Spanish and Portuguese punch of wine and fruit, whose name comes from the word for blood.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Grappa: An Italian brandy distilled from grape pomace, usually around 40 percent alcohol.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Ouzo: A Greek anise spirit that turns milky white when water is added, an effect called the ouzo effect.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Shandy: Beer mixed with lemonade or ginger beer, so it is low in alcohol, a favorite of British pubs.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Mimosa: Champagne with orange juice, a brunch staple, named for the yellow flower of the mimosa tree.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Mulled wine: Red wine warmed with spices such as cinnamon and cloves, served at German Christmas markets as Glühwein.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Pimm's: A gin-based liqueur from the 1840s, served with lemonade and fruit, and the signature drink at Wimbledon.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Port: A sweet fortified wine from Portugal's Douro valley, boosted with grape spirit during fermentation.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Absinthe: A green anise spirit, once banned across Europe and the United States, with a reputation that outran its science.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Bellini: A Prosecco and peach puree cocktail invented in Venice at Harry's Bar, named for the painter Giovanni Bellini.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Root beer: A sweet American soda traditionally made from sassafras, and it is nonalcoholic despite the name.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Ginger ale: A fizzy soft drink, with no alcohol, though it is often used as a cocktail mixer.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Egg cream: Despite the name, a New York soda fountain drink has no eggs or cream, just milk, seltzer and chocolate syrup.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Horchata: A sweet, creamy rice or tiger nut drink, with no alcohol.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Lassi: A yogurt drink from India, nonalcoholic, though bhang lassi in some places is infused with cannabis.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Shirley Temple: A nonalcoholic mix of ginger ale and grenadine, named for the child film star.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Arnold Palmer: Half iced tea and half lemonade, a nonalcoholic drink named for the golfer, who ordered it so often.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Virgin Mary: A Bloody Mary without the vodka, so it has tomato juice and spices but no alcohol.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Cream soda: A vanilla-flavored soda that contains no alcohol, and typically no cream.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Birch beer: A soda made with birch bark flavoring, popular in Pennsylvania, and it has no alcohol.
Drinks that contain alcohol.Tonic water: A bitter soft drink with quinine, originally taken to prevent malaria, and it contains no alcohol.

Ancient sites in Mexico.Chichen Itza: The Maya city's El Castillo pyramid is aligned so that at equinoxes a shadow shaped like a serpent seems to slither down its stairs.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Teotihuacan: Centuries before the Aztecs, this city had perhaps 100,000 people. The Aztecs found the ruins and named it the place where gods were created.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Tulum: A Maya walled port city perched on cliffs above the Caribbean, which was still occupied when Spaniards arrived.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Palenque: Its Temple of Inscriptions holds the tomb of King Pakal, who ruled for about 68 years in the 7th century.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Monte Albán: Built on a levelled mountaintop by the Zapotecs around 500 BC, with a plaza carved with mysterious dancer figures.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Uxmal: A Maya city with the Pyramid of the Magician, with rounded corners, and noted for its Puuc-style stone mosaics.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Calakmul: A giant Maya city in jungle near the Guatemalan border, with a huge pyramid, once a rival of Tikal.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Cobá: A Maya site in Quintana Roo whose Nohoch Mul is one of the tallest pyramids on the Yucatán; it was once climbable, though no longer.
Ancient sites in Mexico.El Tajín: A Totonac city in Veracruz known for the Pyramid of the Niches, with 365 recesses, and its ball courts.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Machu Picchu: The Inca citadel was built around 1450 and sits high in the Peruvian Andes, so it's South American.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Tikal: A major Maya city, with temples rising above the canopy, in the rainforest of Guatemala, not Mexico.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Copán: A Maya city in Honduras, known for its elaborately carved stelae and a hieroglyphic stairway.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Caral: A Peruvian city about 5,000 years old, one of the oldest in the Americas, which flourished without pottery.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Nazca Lines: Giant desert drawings in Peru of animals and shapes, made some 2,000 years ago, best viewed from the air.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Sacsayhuamán: An Inca fortress above Cusco, Peru, built from enormous stones, some weighing over 100 tonnes, fitted tightly.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Chan Chan: The largest adobe city in the Americas, built by Peru's Chimú, covering around 20 square kilometres.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Tiwanaku: A Bolivian city near Lake Titicaca whose Gateway of the Sun is carved from a single block of stone.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Easter Island: Chile's remote Pacific island, with nearly 900 giant moai statues made by the Rapa Nui people.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Stonehenge: England's prehistoric stone circle, begun about 5,000 years ago, whose giant bluestones were brought from Wales.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Angkor Wat: Cambodia's temple complex is a southeast Asian wonder, far from Mexico's ancient cities.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Pyramids of Giza: Egypt's Great Pyramid was the tallest building on Earth for nearly 4,000 years.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Petra: Jordan's rock-cut Nabataean city, which has no connection to ancient Mexico.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Mesa Verde: Cliff dwellings in Colorado built by the Ancestral Puebloans, an ancient site of the United States, not Mexico.
Ancient sites in Mexico.Altun Ha: A Maya site in Belize, whose jade head of the sun god is the largest known carved jade Maya object.

Places in South Africa.Cape Town: Table Mountain looms over it, and it is the only major city with a floral kingdom, the Cape Floristic Region, within its borders.
Places in South Africa.Johannesburg: Born from an 1886 gold rush, it is often called the largest city in the world not on a river, lake or coast.
Places in South Africa.Durban: Home to the largest Indian population outside India, and its beachfront Golden Mile draws surfers year-round.
Places in South Africa.Pretoria: South Africa's executive capital is famous for jacaranda trees that turn its streets purple each October, giving it the nickname Jacaranda City.
Places in South Africa.Table Mountain: This flat-topped peak is covered by a cloud called the tablecloth, and the mountain hosts more plant species than the entire British Isles.
Places in South Africa.Kruger: This national park, about the size of Wales, protects the Big Five and was founded in 1926 as one of Africa's oldest reserves.
Places in South Africa.Robben Island: Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 prison years here, and the island is now a World Heritage Site.
Places in South Africa.Cape of Good Hope: Despite its fame, it isn't Africa's southernmost point; that honor goes to Cape Agulhas, about 150 km southeast.
Places in South Africa.Soweto: This township near Johannesburg saw the 1976 student uprising, and its Vilakazi Street housed two Nobel Peace laureates, Mandela and Tutu.
Places in South Africa.Stellenbosch: South Africa's second-oldest European settlement, founded in 1679, it is the heart of a winelands region and a leading university town.
Places in South Africa.Garden Route: This scenic coastal stretch of forests, lagoons and beaches along the southern coast runs between Mossel Bay and the Storms River.
Places in South Africa.Drakensberg: Its name means Dragon Mountains in Afrikaans, and its cliffs hold thousands of San rock paintings.
Places in South Africa.Victoria Falls: It lies on the Zambia-Zimbabwe border, not South Africa, and locals call it Mosi-oa-Tunya, the Smoke That Thunders.
Places in South Africa.Okavango Delta: A Botswana wonder: this inland delta floods in the dry season, drawing huge wildlife herds.
Places in South Africa.Etosha: Namibia's famous national park centers on a vast salt pan so large it can be seen from space.
Places in South Africa.Windhoek: The capital of Namibia, known for German colonial architecture and a notable local beer tradition.
Places in South Africa.Gaborone: The capital of Botswana, a country that rose from poverty to wealth thanks to diamonds, not South African territory.
Places in South Africa.Harare: Zimbabwe's capital, once called Salisbury, has more than 1,000 meters of elevation, which keeps its climate mild.
Places in South Africa.Serengeti: A trap for safari lovers: it is in Tanzania, famous for the annual wildebeest migration of over a million animals.
Places in South Africa.Kilimanjaro: Africa's highest peak, at about 5,895 meters, is in Tanzania, and its glaciers have shrunk dramatically.
Places in South Africa.Maputo: Mozambique's capital sits on a bay, and its railway station was once said to be designed by Gustave Eiffel's firm.
Places in South Africa.Maseru: The capital of Lesotho, a kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa, so it is a trap despite being just next door.
Places in South Africa.Mbabane: Eswatini's administrative capital, in a kingdom bordering South Africa, is nestled in the Dlangeni Hills.
Places in South Africa.Zanzibar: This Tanzanian island was once the center of the spice and slave trades and gave Freddie Mercury his birthplace.

Places in Switzerland.Zurich: Switzerland's largest city and a global banking center, where the Dada art movement was founded in 1916.
Places in Switzerland.Geneva: Home to the Red Cross and many UN agencies, and its Jet d'Eau fountain shoots water about 140 meters high.
Places in Switzerland.Bern: The capital, perhaps surprisingly, is not Zurich; Switzerland officially has no capital in law, and Bern is the federal city.
Places in Switzerland.Lucerne: Its covered wooden Chapel Bridge dates to 1333, and a famous dying lion is carved into a rock face nearby.
Places in Switzerland.Interlaken: Sits between two lakes, Thun and Brienz, and is the gateway to the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau peaks.
Places in Switzerland.Zermatt: This car-free resort lies below the Matterhorn, the pyramid peak at over 4,400 meters, a mountain first climbed in 1865.
Places in Switzerland.Basel: On the Rhine near the French and German borders, it hosts the world's major art fair, Art Basel, and has pharmaceutical giants.
Places in Switzerland.Lausanne: The home of the International Olympic Committee, which has been based here since 1915.
Places in Switzerland.St. Moritz: A glitzy Engadin resort that hosted the Winter Olympics twice, in 1928 and 1948, and claims 300 days of sun.
Places in Switzerland.Davos: The Alpine town where the World Economic Forum meets each January, at over 1,500 meters among Europe's highest cities.
Places in Switzerland.Lugano: A lakeside city in the Italian-speaking canton of Ticino, with palm trees and a Mediterranean feel.
Places in Switzerland.Montreux: Home of the famous jazz festival, and Freddie Mercury's statue stands on its lakeside promenade.
Places in Switzerland.Innsbruck: An Austrian city in the Alps that hosted the Winter Olympics in 1964 and 1976, not Swiss.
Places in Switzerland.Salzburg: Mozart's Austrian birthplace and the setting for The Sound of Music.
Places in Switzerland.Chamonix: A French resort at the foot of Mont Blanc, the first Winter Olympics host in 1924.
Places in Switzerland.Vaduz: The capital of Liechtenstein, a tiny country between Switzerland and Austria.
Places in Switzerland.Garmisch: A Bavarian resort in Germany beneath the Zugspitze, hosted the 1936 Winter Olympics.
Places in Switzerland.Lake Como: An Italian lake in Lombardy, celebrity-filled and shaped like an upside-down Y.
Places in Switzerland.Annecy: A French lakeside town in the Alps, nicknamed the Venice of the Alps for its canals.
Places in Switzerland.Strasbourg: A French city on the Rhine border with Germany, seat of the European Parliament.
Places in Switzerland.Kitzbühel: An Austrian ski town, famous for the Hahnenkamm downhill race, one of skiing's most dangerous.
Places in Switzerland.Bolzano: An Italian city in South Tyrol, where Ötzi the Iceman mummy is on display.
Places in Switzerland.Grenoble: A French city in the Alps that hosted the 1968 Winter Olympics.
Places in Switzerland.Milan: Italy's fashion capital, home to La Scala opera and Leonardo's Last Supper, just south of the Swiss border.

Found in the Netherlands.Amsterdam: The capital sits largely below sea level, with more than 100 kilometers of canals and over a million bikes in the metro area.
Found in the Netherlands.Rotterdam: Europe's largest port, almost entirely rebuilt after bombing in 1940, with bold modern architecture like the Cube Houses.
Found in the Netherlands.The Hague: The seat of government and not the capital, it hosts the International Court of Justice and the Peace Palace.
Found in the Netherlands.Utrecht: Its Dom Tower is the country's tallest church tower, and its canals have unusual lower-level wharf cellars.
Found in the Netherlands.Keukenhof: The world's largest flower garden plants about seven million bulbs each year, open only for a couple of spring months.
Found in the Netherlands.Rijksmuseum: Amsterdam's national museum holds Rembrandt's Night Watch and Vermeer's Milkmaid, and its cycling path passes right through the building.
Found in the Netherlands.Anne Frank House: The canal-side hiding place where Anne wrote her diary draws more than a million visitors a year, behind a swinging bookcase.
Found in the Netherlands.Kinderdijk: Nineteen 18th-century windmills in a World Heritage polder, built to pump water out of low-lying land.
Found in the Netherlands.Zaanse Schans: A living museum of working windmills, clogs and cheese, set beside the Zaan river.
Found in the Netherlands.Delft: Home of blue-and-white Delftware pottery and of Vermeer, who painted here in the 1600s.
Found in the Netherlands.Maastricht: The southern city where the 1992 treaty that created the euro was signed, and a Roman-era stronghold.
Found in the Netherlands.Eindhoven: A technology hub, home of Philips, which began making light bulbs here in 1891.
Found in the Netherlands.Antwerp: A Belgian port city, the world's diamond trading center, home of Rubens.
Found in the Netherlands.Bruges: A medieval Belgian city of canals and lace, nicknamed the Venice of the North.
Found in the Netherlands.Ghent: A Belgian city of castles and canals, with the Ghent Altarpiece by van Eyck.
Found in the Netherlands.Brussels: Belgium's capital hosts the EU's main institutions and boasts the country's waffles and chocolate.
Found in the Netherlands.Atomium: A Brussels landmark built for the 1958 World's Fair, a huge model of an iron crystal, so it belongs to Belgium.
Found in the Netherlands.Manneken Pis: A small bronze boy statue in Brussels, in Belgium, with a wardrobe of hundreds of costumes.
Found in the Netherlands.Liège: A Belgian city known for waffles and for a hilltop staircase of 374 steps.
Found in the Netherlands.Luxembourg: A tiny grand duchy between Belgium, France and Germany, one of the world's wealthiest countries.
Found in the Netherlands.Cologne: A German city on the Rhine, famous for its cathedral and eau de cologne.
Found in the Netherlands.Aachen: A German spa city near the Dutch border, where Charlemagne was buried.
Found in the Netherlands.Lille: A French city near the Belgian border with a strongly Flemish feel; it is the birthplace of Charles de Gaulle.
Found in the Netherlands.Düsseldorf: A German city on the Rhine, famous for its Altbier and fashion trade, across the border from the Netherlands.

Tectonic plates.Pacific: The largest plate, mostly under the ocean. Around its edge runs the Ring of Fire, where most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes occur.
Tectonic plates.North American: This plate carries most of North America and part of the Atlantic floor. It's drifting away from Europe by a couple of centimeters a year.
Tectonic plates.Eurasian: A huge plate carrying Europe and most of Asia. It's slowly colliding with India and the Arabian plate, creating the Himalayas.
Tectonic plates.African: The African plate is slowly splitting in the East African Rift. In millions of years, a new ocean could separate East Africa.
Tectonic plates.Antarctic: The plate under Antarctica is surrounded by spreading ridges. It's almost entirely covered with ice, and is nearly stationary relative to the pole.
Tectonic plates.South American: The plate carrying South America is grinding against the Nazca plate, which builds the Andes. Its eastern edge is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Tectonic plates.Nazca: A plate in the eastern Pacific diving beneath South America. This subduction creates the Andes and the Chilean earthquakes.
Tectonic plates.Philippine Sea: A plate near Japan and the Philippines. It subducts beneath neighbors, forming the deep Mariana Trench region.
Tectonic plates.Arabian: The plate beneath the Arabian Peninsula, pushing north into Eurasia. It's behind the Zagros Mountains of Iran.
Tectonic plates.Caribbean: A relatively small plate under the Caribbean Sea. Its motion helps explain the region's earthquakes and volcanoes.
Tectonic plates.Cocos: A small plate off Central America that dives under the Caribbean plate. It feeds the volcanoes of Mexico and Central America.
Tectonic plates.Juan de Fuca: A small plate off the northwest coast of North America. It sinks under the continent and could trigger a major earthquake in the Cascadia zone.
Tectonic plates.Scotia: A small plate near the southern tip of South America, in the Scotia Sea. It lies between the South American and Antarctic plates.
Tectonic plates.Atlantic: An ocean, not a plate. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through it, with the North American and Eurasian plates meeting there.
Tectonic plates.Arctic: An ocean, not a plate. The seafloor beneath it belongs to the North American and Eurasian plates.
Tectonic plates.Hawaiian: Hawaii sits in the middle of the Pacific plate, over a hotspot, not on a plate boundary. The islands are a chain formed as the plate moved.
Tectonic plates.Himalayan: The Himalayas are mountains, not a plate. They're raised by the Indian plate's push into Eurasia, and are still growing.
Tectonic plates.Greenland: An island rather than a plate. It sits on the North American plate.
Tectonic plates.Iceland: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates part. It isn't a plate of its own, though it's splitting in two.
Tectonic plates.Mediterranean: A sea rather than a plate. Its floor is a patchwork of the African and Eurasian plates colliding, which makes the region quake.
Tectonic plates.Siberian: A region of Russia, not a plate. It sits on the Eurasian plate.
Tectonic plates.Sahara: A desert, not a plate. It's part of the African plate.
Tectonic plates.Amazon: A river and rainforest. It sits on the South American plate.
Tectonic plates.Alaskan: Alaska isn't a plate. It sits on the North American plate, which the Pacific plate dives beneath.

Inventions credited to women.Windshield wiper: Mary Anderson patented a hand-operated wiper in 1903 after watching a streetcar driver struggle in sleet. Carmakers initially dismissed it.
Inventions credited to women.Dishwasher: Josephine Cochrane built the first practical one in the 1880s because servants kept chipping her china. Her company later became part of KitchenAid.
Inventions credited to women.Kevlar: Chemist Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont spotted the odd, cloudy liquid in 1965. It spun into fibers about five times stronger than steel by weight.
Inventions credited to women.Toll House cookie: Ruth Wakefield, who ran the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts, is credited with the chocolate chip cookie in the 1930s. Nestlé later bought her recipe.
Inventions credited to women.Liquid Paper: Secretary Bette Nesmith Graham first mixed white paint in her kitchen blender to cover typing errors. Her son Michael later became a Monkee.
Inventions credited to women.Coffee filter: Melitta Bentz, a German housewife, punched holes in a brass pot and lined it with blotting paper in 1908. Her company still bears her name.
Inventions credited to women.Car heater: Margaret Wilcox patented a heater powered by the engine's own warmth around 1893, a long time before heated cabins became standard.
Inventions credited to women.Paper bag machine: Margaret Knight designed a machine making flat-bottomed paper bags in the 1870s and won a patent fight against a man who had copied it.
Inventions credited to women.Frequency hopping: Actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil patented it in 1942 to stop torpedo jamming. The idea later underpinned Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
Inventions credited to women.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell won the patent in 1876, with Elisha Gray filing a rival claim the same day. Not a women's invention, so it's a trap.
Inventions credited to women.Light bulb: Edison gets the fame, but Joseph Swan in Britain built a working bulb around the same time. Both men, so it doesn't belong here.
Inventions credited to women.Airplane: The Wright brothers flew first at Kitty Hawk in 1903. Their sister Katharine helped fund and support them, but the invention itself is credited to the men.
Inventions credited to women.Radio: Marconi, Tesla and others are all credited in the radio story. Despite the crowd of claimants, none of them was a woman.
Inventions credited to women.Television: Mechanical and electronic TV grew from work by Baird and Philo Farnsworth in the 1920s. Farnsworth sketched his idea as a teenager on a farm.
Inventions credited to women.Steam engine: Thomas Newcomen and James Watt are the names tied to it. Watt's separate condenser made it efficient, and the unit of power is named after him.
Inventions credited to women.Printing press: Gutenberg's movable-type press, around 1450, is credited to a man. It made the Bible one of the first books mass-produced in Europe.
Inventions credited to women.Telescope: The first patent request came from Dutch spectacle maker Hans Lippershey in 1608. Galileo heard of it and built his own within a year.
Inventions credited to women.Bicycle: Karl von Drais built his pedal-less running machine in 1817, and pedals came later. No woman is credited with the bicycle itself.
Inventions credited to women.Zipper: Whitcomb Judson and later Gideon Sundback are the zipper's men. The name zipper came from a rubber boots brand that adopted it.
Inventions credited to women.Velcro: Swiss engineer George de Mestral invented it after burrs clung to his dog's fur in the 1940s. A man's invention, not a woman's.
Inventions credited to women.Microwave oven: Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket near a radar tube in the 1940s. His first commercial oven was nearly six feet tall.
Inventions credited to women.Computer mouse: Douglas Engelbart demonstrated the mouse in 1968, and the first one was carved from wood. The name came from its tail-like cord.
Inventions credited to women.World Wide Web: Tim Berners-Lee proposed it at CERN in 1989. He famously never patented it, which is why anyone can build on the web freely.
Inventions credited to women.Telegraph: Samuel Morse and others developed it in the 1830s and 40s. His first public message in 1844 was 'What hath God wrought'.

Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Jaws: Spielberg's 1975 shark thriller is often called the first summer blockbuster. The mechanical shark kept breaking, so it appears little.
The 1982 film became the highest-grossing movie of its time. Spielberg shot it mostly from a child's eye level.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Jurassic Park: The 1993 film's dinosaurs mixed animatronics with early CGI, and its T. rex roar blended elephant, tiger and alligator sounds.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Schindler's List: Spielberg shot it in black and white in Poland in 1993, winning Best Picture and his first Best Director Oscar.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Hook: This 1991 Peter Pan sequel stars Robin Williams as a grown-up Peter and Dustin Hoffman as Captain Hook.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Lincoln: Daniel Day-Lewis won his third Best Actor Oscar for the 2012 film, a record. It focuses on passing the 13th Amendment.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.War Horse: This 2011 film is based on a children's novel and stage play, which used life-size puppet horses.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Munich: This 2005 thriller dramatizes Israel's response to the 1972 Olympics massacre. It was nominated for Best Picture.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Minority Report: The 2002 sci-fi film, based on Philip K. Dick, stars Tom Cruise. It's famous for its gesture-controlled screens, which inspired real tech.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Catch Me If You Can: This 2002 film is based on conman Frank Abagnale Jr., who faked being a pilot, doctor and lawyer as a teen. Parts of the real story are disputed.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Saving Private Ryan: The opening Omaha Beach landing took about 25 minutes, and veterans reportedly found it so realistic it was hard to watch.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.The Fabelmans: This 2022 film is Spielberg's semi-autobiographical story, about a boy who falls in love with filmmaking.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Duel: Made in 1971 for TV, this thriller about a truck chasing a driver was Spielberg's early breakthrough and was released in cinemas abroad.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Star Wars: George Lucas directed the 1977 film. Spielberg and Lucas are friends, and they worked together on Indiana Jones.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Gremlins: Joe Dante directed this 1984 film, produced by Spielberg. He's a producer here, not the director.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Back to the Future: Robert Zemeckis directed it in 1985, with Spielberg as executive producer. Michael J. Fox replaced Eric Stoltz early in shooting.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.The Goonies: Richard Donner directed this 1985 adventure from a Spielberg story. His name is on it as a producer, not director.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Titanic: James Cameron's 1997 epic won 11 Oscars, tying a record. Spielberg had nothing to do with it.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Avatar: James Cameron directed Avatar in 2009, for years the top-grossing film ever. Not Spielberg.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Ghostbusters: Ivan Reitman directed the 1984 comedy. Not Spielberg, though it's of that era.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Men in Black: Barry Sonnenfeld directed the 1997 film. Spielberg was executive producer, so it's a classic trap.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Twister: Jan de Bont directed it in 1996, with Spielberg's company among producers. Not his direction.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Inception: Christopher Nolan directed this 2010 film and wrote its spinning-top ending. Not Spielberg.
Films directed by Steven Spielberg.Jumanji: Joe Johnston directed the 1995 original. Spielberg was not involved, and it was based on a Chris Van Allsburg book.

Studio Ghibli films.Spirited Away: Hayao Miyazaki's 2001 film won the Best Animated Feature Oscar and for years was Japan's highest-grossing film ever.
Studio Ghibli films.My Neighbor Totoro: Totoro became Studio Ghibli's mascot and appears in its logo, and the forest spirit has little screen time in his own film.
Studio Ghibli films.Princess Mononoke: The 1997 epic about a forest war set a Japanese box-office record at the time and kept Miyazaki working by hand.
Studio Ghibli films.Ponyo: Ponyo is a loose retelling of The Little Mermaid, and Miyazaki's team drew most of its waves by hand.
Studio Ghibli films.Howl's Moving Castle: The film is based on a novel by British author Diana Wynne Jones, and was Miyazaki's 2004 film.

Famous movie spaceships.Ecto-1: The Ghostbusters' car is a converted 1959 Cadillac ambulance-hearse, so not a spaceship.

Noises your body can make.Hiccup: Charles Osborne hiccupped for roughly 68 years, from 1922 until 1990, per Guinness.
Noises your body can make.Sneeze: Most people shut their eyes during a sneeze by reflex, but keeping them open is possible, and eyeballs popping out is a myth.
Noises your body can make.Burp: A burp is swallowed air escaping, nothing more.
Noises your body can make.Snore: Snoring comes from the soft tissues in your throat vibrating as you breathe in your sleep.
Noises your body can make.Cough: A cough is a reflex that clears the airway, triggered by nerves before you decide.
Noises your body can make.Knuckle crack: Dr Donald Unger cracked only his left hand's knuckles for 60 years and won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2009 for showing no arthritis.
Noises your body can make.Tummy rumble: The medical term for a stomach rumble is borborygmi, and it happens even when you're full.
Noises your body can make.Hum: You can hum with your mouth shut because sound escapes through your nose.
Noises your body can make.Whistle: Whistling can be a language: Silbo Gomero on the Canary island of La Gomera, which locals use over valleys.
Noises your body can make.Clap: Hands cupped together trap air, and the sudden escape makes the clap.
Noises your body can make.Laugh: Rats giggle in ultrasound when tickled, which scientists have measured.
Noises your body can make.Sigh: A sigh resets tiny air sacs in your lungs, and some researchers believe that's its job.
Noises your body can make.Gulp: A gulp is a swallow of air or liquid, loud when your throat is dry.
Noises your body can make.Blink: A blink is silent and happens roughly 15 times a minute.
Noises your body can make.Shiver: A shiver is rapid muscle contractions, generating heat in silence.
Noises your body can make.Blush: Blushing is only a reddening of the face, and Darwin called it the most peculiar human expression.
Noises your body can make.Sweat: Sweat is almost odorless until skin bacteria break it down, and it's quiet.
Noises your body can make.Wink: A wink is silent, and many people can't do it with one eye alone.
Noises your body can make.Frown: A frown is silent, and cultures read it the same way.
Noises your body can make.Smile: A smile is silent, and even people blind from birth smile.
Noises your body can make.Nod: A nod is silent, though in Bulgaria nodding traditionally means no.
Noises your body can make.Stretch: A stretch is silent, though a yawn with a stretch is called pandiculation.
Noises your body can make.Goosebumps: Goosebumps are tiny muscles tugging hairs upright, a leftover from furry ancestors, and they're silent.
Noises your body can make.Squint: A squint narrows your eyes to cut out blur, and it makes no noise.

Tools a medieval scribe used.Quill: Usually a goose feather; feathers from the left wing curve away from a right-handed writer's view, which made them preferred.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Parchment: Made from scraped, stretched sheep or goat skin, so a large book might need a whole flock's hides.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Ink: Iron gall ink, from oak galls and iron salts, slowly bit into the page and could even eat through it over centuries.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Penknife: It's why it has that name: scribes used it to sharpen their quills and to scrape away mistakes.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Vellum: Fine calfskin so costly that old manuscripts were often scraped clean and reused, leaving ghostly writing underneath.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Gold leaf: Hammered paper-thin and burnished onto the page, it made 'illuminated' manuscripts glow in candlelight.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Pumice: Scribes rubbed it on parchment to smooth the surface, and it helped to remove stray blots.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Inkhorn: A cow's horn that held ink, which also gave us 'inkhorn terms', the show-off words scholars loved in the 1500s.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Wax tablet: Reusable wax-coated boards were used for drafts and notes before the final text went onto costly parchment.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Stylus: One end was pointed for scratching letters into wax and the other flat for smoothing them out; the Latin 'stilus' gave us 'style'.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Ballpoint pen: Inventor László Bíró patented it in 1938 in Hungary, and scribes dipped quills.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Graphite pencil: Scribes used a lead or metal point to rule faint guide lines, but the wood-cased graphite pencil came in the 1500s.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Typewriter: The first commercial typewriter came in the 1860s, so a scribe's output was entirely handwritten.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Rubber eraser: Joseph Priestley noted in 1770 that rubber rubs out pencil marks, hence the British word rubber; scribes scraped instead.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Paper clip: It appeared in the late 1800s, and scribes bound pages by sewing them.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Stapler: The common stapler appeared in the late 1800s, and medieval scribes sewed their pages.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Highlighter: Carter's Hi-Liter appeared in 1963, so a scribe emphasised words with red ink, called rubrics.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Printer: Gutenberg's press of about 1450 began putting scribes out of work, and computer printers came centuries later.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Sticky notes: 3M's Post-it grew from a weak glue found in 1968 by Spencer Silver and reached stores in 1980.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Correction fluid: Invented in the 1950s by secretary Bette Nesmith Graham, whose son Mike was in The Monkees.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Felt-tip pen: Japan's first fibre-tip pens appeared in the early 1960s, and scribes used quills.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Hole punch: Scribes pricked small holes to guide ruling lines, but the paper hole punch is an 1880s German invention.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Sharpie: Introduced in 1964, the Sharpie came centuries after the quill, and ink was iron gall.
Tools a medieval scribe used.Thumbtack: Edwin Moore patented the push-pin in 1900, and medieval pages were sewn, not pinned.

Things that come in a squeeze tube.Caulk: Caulk seals gaps around tubs and windows, keeping out water.
Things that come in a squeeze tube.Antibiotic ointment: Antibiotic ointments help prevent infection in small cuts and scrapes.
Things that come in a squeeze tube.Wasabi: Most tube 'wasabi' is actually horseradish with mustard and coloring, since real wasabi is hard to grow.
Things that come in a squeeze tube.Hair gel: Hair gel was a staple of the 1980s, holding hair in place with polymers that dry stiff.
Things that come in a squeeze tube.Milk: Milk once came in glass bottles delivered to the door, and cartons arrived in the 1930s.
Things that come in a squeeze tube.Soda: Soda comes in cans and bottles, and a can's pull tab was a 1960s invention.

Things that come in a squeeze tube.Bread: Bread comes in loaves, and sliced bread first sold in the 1920s.
