Things that have a hinge.Laptop: Laptop hinges are stress tested for tens of thousands of open-close cycles, and the hinge is a classic point of failure.
Things that have a hinge.Cupboard: Cupboard doors often use concealed cup hinges with a spring and screws that let you adjust the alignment.
Things that have a hinge.Garden gate: A garden gate sags over time because its weight pulls on the top hinge; a diagonal brace stops the droop.
Things that have a hinge.Toilet seat: Toilet seat hinges are made of plastic or stainless steel, and slow-close ones use a tiny damper.
Things that have a hinge.Eyeglasses: The tiny hinge on eyeglasses is held by a screw that famously works loose, which is why repair kits are small.
Things that have a hinge.Flip phone: Flip phones put their screen and keypad on a hinge, and foldable smartphones revived the idea in the 2020s.
Things that have a hinge.Jewelry box: Jewelry boxes often use a small brass hinge, and some play a tune when you open the lid.
Things that have a hinge.Mailbox: A mailbox flap swings on a hinge, and the standard US box with a pull-down door dates back to 1915.
Things that have a hinge.Piano lid: A grand piano's lid is propped open on a stick, and its hinge lets the sound escape into the room.
Things that have a hinge.Book: A book has a spine, which flexes like a hinge, though technically the binding flexes instead of a metal piece.
Things that have a hinge.Drawer: A drawer slides on runners rather than swinging on a hinge, which is why it moves straight out.
Things that have a hinge.Sliding door: A sliding door rides on a track and rollers; it does not swing open, so there is no hinge.
Things that have a hinge.Spoon: A spoon is one solid piece of metal with no joints, so it has no hinge.
Things that have a hinge.Rug: A rug is a flat woven piece of fabric, which flexes everywhere and needs no hinge.
Things that have a hinge.Plate: A plate is one rigid piece, and there is nothing in it that swings.
Things that have a hinge.Pillow: A pillow is soft stuffing in a cover, with no mechanism of any kind.
Things that have a hinge.Curtain: Curtains hang from rings on a rod and slide along it, so they move without a hinge.
Things that have a hinge.Scarf: A scarf is soft, flexible fabric that bends anywhere, so a hinge would be pointless.
Things that have a hinge.Brick: A brick is a solid rigid block, so it has no moving parts.
Things that have a hinge.Towel: A towel is flexible cloth and has no hinge, though it may hang from a hinged rack.
Things that have a hinge.Pencil: A pencil is a solid wooden rod around a graphite core with no moving parts.
Things that have a hinge.Mug: A mug is a single molded piece; a travel mug lid may flip on a tiny hinge, though.
Things that have a hinge.Balloon: A balloon is a thin rubber skin that stretches and has no hinge or rigid parts.

Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Cooking grease: Grease cools and solidifies in pipes, and combined with wipes it forms fatbergs, like the 130-ton one found in London's sewers.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Coffee grounds: Coffee grounds clump and stay in pipes, and they pile up into a stubborn sludge; compost them instead.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Paint thinner: Paint thinner is hazardous waste, since it is toxic and flammable and can harm water treatment systems.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Bacon fat: Bacon fat is liquid when hot but sets hard as it cools, so it can clog the drain within days.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Cat litter: Cat litter, especially clumping clay, swells with water and can set like cement in pipes.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Wet wipes: Wet wipes marked flushable usually don't break down, and they are a leading cause of sewer blockages.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Motor oil: Motor oil can foul a huge amount of water from a small spill, and used oil can be re-refined, so take it to a recycling point.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Expired medicine: Medicine in the water supply can reach rivers and affect fish, so use drug take-back programs.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Cooked pasta: Cooked pasta swells and clumps with starch, and it can plug a drain trap.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Flour: Flour mixes with water into a paste that is a sticky glue, which builds up in pipes.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Concrete mix: Concrete mix sets hard in drains and ruins your plumbing, a problem even a plumber may find hard to fix.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Tap water: Tap water is what sinks are made for, and you can pour as much as you like.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Dish soap: Dish soap is formulated to rinse down the drain, and it also cuts through grease.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Hand soap: Soap goes down the drain by design, and it works because its molecules grab both oil and water.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Toothpaste: Toothpaste in small amounts is fine for the sink, though don't pour out large amounts.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Mouthwash: Mouthwash is made to be spat out and goes down the drain.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Shower gel: Shower gel washes away in water, and it is made to be rinsed.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Shampoo: Shampoo is designed to be rinsed away, though hair clogs are the real drain enemy.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Vinegar: Vinegar is a classic drain cleaner, and with baking soda it fizzes to loosen light buildup.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Lemon juice: Lemon juice is a mild acid that freshens drains, and it is safe for pipes.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Salt water: Salt water is fine for the drain, but the sodium is one reason it is not great for the garden.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Baking soda: Baking soda can be poured down a drain to deodorize, and it is mild and safe.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Rinse water: Rinse water is what a sink is for, so it flows right through.
Things you shouldn't pour down the sink.Sparkling water: Sparkling water is just water with dissolved carbon dioxide, which makes it perfectly fine to pour out.

Body parts spelled with three letters.Arm: The arm has three main bones in total, and a human arm's reach is roughly equal to your height.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Leg: The leg holds the longest bone in the body, the femur, and the legs make up about half your height.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Eye: Eyes can tell apart about a million colors, yet each one has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Ear: The ear includes the smallest bones in the body, and it also helps with balance.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Hip: The hip joint is a ball-and-socket, which gives it a wide range of motion, and it carries your body weight.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Lip: Lips have more nerve endings than most other body parts, which is why they feel so sensitive.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Toe: The big toe helps you balance and push off when you walk. People often don't notice how important it is.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Rib: Humans typically have 24 ribs, 12 on each side, and they flex slightly when you breathe.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Jaw: The jaw is the only moving bone of the skull, and its masseter muscle is among the strongest in the body for its size.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Gum: Gum is the soft tissue around the teeth. It is also what you chew: chicle, a tree sap from Mexico, was the original base.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Chin: Chin has four letters, and it's the bony front of the lower jaw, which only humans have prominently.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Shin: Shin has four letters, and the tibia beneath it is the second-longest bone in the body.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Neck: Neck has four letters, and it holds seven vertebrae, the same as a giraffe.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Knee: Knee has four letters, and the kneecap is the largest sesamoid bone in the body.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Nose: Nose has four letters, and your nose can tell apart a vast number of smells.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Hand: Hand has four letters, and it has 27 bones.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Foot: Foot has four letters, so it misses the cut. Each foot has 26 bones, so both feet hold about a quarter of all your bones.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Head: Head has four letters, and an adult head weighs about 5 kilograms.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Back: Back has four letters, and the spine holds 33 vertebrae.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Palm: Palm has four letters, so it misses. The tree is named for its leaves, which look like a spread hand.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Heel: Heel has four letters, and the heel bone is the largest in the foot.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Brow: Brow has four letters, and it helps keep sweat out of your eyes.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Lung: Lung has four letters, and your lungs hold roughly six liters of air at full capacity.
Body parts spelled with three letters.Calf: Calf has four letters, and the word also names a baby cow.

Ways to describe pain.Throbbing: A throbbing pain often beats in time with your pulse because the swollen tissue is pressing against blood vessels.
Ways to describe pain.Stabbing: Stabbing pain is quick, sharp and localized, and doctors listen closely to this description, because it can hint at nerve irritation.
Ways to describe pain.Aching: An ache is a dull, constant pain, and the word was pronounced aitch until Shakespeare's time, when it rhymed with the letter H.
Ways to describe pain.Burning: Burning pain is typical of nerve damage, such as shingles or diabetic neuropathy, and capsaicin in chili triggers the same nerves.
Ways to describe pain.Sharp: Sharp pain is often a sign that tissue is being damaged right now, so it makes you pull away before more harm occurs.
Ways to describe pain.Dull: Dull pain comes from deeper tissues like muscles and organs and is hard to place exactly, in contrast to a sharp pain.
Ways to describe pain.Shooting: Shooting pain, like sciatica, travels along a nerve, and it can streak from the lower back down the leg.
Ways to describe pain.Stinging: A stinging pain is fast and surface-level, like that from a bee, and it is caused by fast-conducting nerve fibers in the skin.
Ways to describe pain.Cramping: Cramps come from a muscle that tightens involuntarily, and doctors still aren't fully certain why nighttime leg cramps happen.
Ways to describe pain.Searing: Searing means scorching, from the idea of branding with hot iron, and it suggests an intense burning pain.
Ways to describe pain.Sore: Sore comes from the Old English sar, meaning painful, and it is the same word as sorry in its roots.
Ways to describe pain.Pounding: A pounding headache gets its hammer feeling from blood vessels in the head pulsing, especially in migraines.
Ways to describe pain.Soothing: Soothing used to mean confirming as true, since the word comes from Old English soth, truth, and now it means easing pain, not describing it.
Ways to describe pain.Comfortable: Comfortable comes from Latin for strengthening greatly, and it now means free from pain, so not a way to describe pain.
Ways to describe pain.Relaxed: Relaxed means loosened, and relaxation is used to ease pain, but it is not a descriptor of pain itself.
Ways to describe pain.Calm: Calm may come from the Greek kauma, the heat of the day, because it was a time to rest in a hot climate.
Ways to describe pain.Cozy: Cozy is a Scottish word that may have been imported to English in the 1700s, and it is the opposite of painful.
Ways to describe pain.Pleasant: Pleasant is a pleasing feeling, so it is the opposite of describing pain.
Ways to describe pain.Painless: Painless literally means without pain, so it is the word that rules pain out rather than describes it.
Ways to describe pain.Restful: Restful describes peace, not pain, and good rest helps your body ease pain by lowering the stress response.
Ways to describe pain.Refreshing: Refreshing describes an invigorating feeling, which is the opposite of how pain feels.
Ways to describe pain.Gentle: Gentle comes from Latin gentilis, of noble birth, and it describes soft touches, not pain.
Ways to describe pain.Fluffy: Fluffy sounds soft and light, like clouds or kittens, and the word has no place among descriptions of pain.
Ways to describe pain.Serene: Serene comes from Latin serenus, clear and calm, and describes tranquil states, not suffering.

Pioneers of medicine.Florence Nightingale: Nightingale used statistical charts to show that soldiers died more from poor sanitation than wounds, and became the first woman in the Royal Society of Statistics.
Pioneers of medicine.Hippocrates: Called the father of medicine, Hippocrates taught in ancient Greece that diseases have natural causes, and the Hippocratic oath is named for him.
Pioneers of medicine.Louis Pasteur: Pasteur proved germs cause disease, developed vaccines for rabies and anthrax, and his method of heating, pasteurization, is named after him.
Pioneers of medicine.Alexander Fleming: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 when a mold contaminated one of his bacteria dishes and killed the bacteria around it.
Pioneers of medicine.Edward Jenner: Jenner created the first vaccine in 1796 using cowpox to protect against smallpox, and the word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow.
Pioneers of medicine.Jonas Salk: Salk developed the first successful polio vaccine in 1955, and he famously declined to patent it, asking, could you patent the sun?
Pioneers of medicine.Joseph Lister: Lister introduced antiseptic surgery with carbolic acid in the 1860s, and the mouthwash Listerine was named in his honor.
Pioneers of medicine.Elizabeth Blackwell: Blackwell became the first woman to earn a medical degree in the United States in 1849, after being admitted to Geneva College as a joke by students.
Pioneers of medicine.Clara Barton: Barton, known as the angel of the battlefield, tended Civil War soldiers and founded the American Red Cross in 1881.
Pioneers of medicine.Galen: Galen, a Roman-era Greek physician, dissected animals and treated gladiators, and his ideas dominated medicine for over 1,000 years.
Pioneers of medicine.William Harvey: Harvey showed in 1628 that the heart pumps blood in a circuit around the body, overturning ideas from Galen.
Pioneers of medicine.Christiaan Barnard: Barnard performed the world's first human heart transplant in Cape Town in December 1967, and the patient lived for 18 days.
Pioneers of medicine.Isaac Newton: Newton is a titan of physics, with laws of motion and gravity, but not a pioneer of medicine.
Pioneers of medicine.Albert Einstein: Einstein's relativity changed physics, not medicine, though he did help patent an unusual refrigerator.
Pioneers of medicine.Galileo: Galileo's telescope observations backed the idea that Earth orbits the sun, but he is remembered for astronomy, not medicine.
Pioneers of medicine.Thomas Edison: Edison held over 1,000 US patents, including the phonograph, but he was an inventor and not a medical pioneer.
Pioneers of medicine.Nikola Tesla: Tesla's alternating current system powers homes, so he belongs to electrical engineering rather than medicine.
Pioneers of medicine.Copernicus: Copernicus proposed that planets orbit the sun, and was trained in medicine as a young man, but is known for astronomy.
Pioneers of medicine.Archimedes: Archimedes of Syracuse discovered buoyancy and the lever principle, which is mathematics and physics, not medicine.
Pioneers of medicine.Johannes Kepler: Kepler discovered that planets move in ellipses, which is astronomy, not medicine.
Pioneers of medicine.Alan Turing: Turing broke the Enigma code in World War II and laid the groundwork for computing, not medicine.
Pioneers of medicine.Michael Faraday: Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, which led to electric generators, and he was a physicist, not a physician.
Pioneers of medicine.Stephen Hawking: Hawking made cosmic discoveries about black holes, a physics pioneer despite living with ALS, but not a medical one.
Pioneers of medicine.Ada Lovelace: Lovelace wrote what is considered the first computer program in the 1840s, a leap for computing rather than medicine.

Swimming strokes.Freestyle: Freestyle means any stroke, but in practice almost everyone uses front crawl because it is the fastest.
Swimming strokes.Backstroke: Backstroke is the only competitive stroke that starts in the water, and at the 1900 Olympics it was introduced as a race.
Swimming strokes.Breaststroke: Breaststroke is the oldest known stroke, with images dating back to ancient Egypt and Rome, and also the slowest of the four.
Swimming strokes.Butterfly: Butterfly was invented in the 1930s as a variation of breaststroke and became its own Olympic event in 1956.
Swimming strokes.Sidestroke: Sidestroke was the way lifeguards swam for a long time, because it let them keep an eye on a swimmer while moving.
Swimming strokes.Front crawl: Front crawl is the fastest swimming stroke, and the name comes from the way early swimmers observed it in the South Pacific.
Swimming strokes.Doggy paddle: The doggy paddle is the instinctive stroke of toddlers, imitating dogs, and often the first swimming move people ever make.
Swimming strokes.Back crawl: Back crawl is the name used for backstroke in many countries and it alternates arm pulls with a flutter kick.
Swimming strokes.Trudgen: The trudgen, named after English swimmer John Trudgen in the 1870s, was an early overarm stroke and a forerunner of front crawl.
Swimming strokes.Heatstroke: Heatstroke is a dangerous overheating of the body that can be fatal, and it has nothing to do with swimming.
Swimming strokes.Sunstroke: Sunstroke is an old name for heatstroke, from too much time in the sun, and it can strike even swimmers who are in the open.
Swimming strokes.Backhand: Backhand is a stroke in tennis and racket sports, and it shares only the word stroke with swimming.
Swimming strokes.Forehand: A forehand is a tennis stroke, and it is hit on your dominant side, in a different sport from swimming.
Swimming strokes.Treading water: Treading water keeps you afloat in one spot, and it is a survival skill rather than a racing stroke.
Swimming strokes.Uppercut: An uppercut is a boxing punch thrown upward, and boxing is a different sport.
Swimming strokes.Slam dunk: A slam dunk in basketball was banned in college play from 1967 to 1976, and it is not a swimming stroke.
Swimming strokes.Lay-up: A lay-up is a close-range basketball shot, so it is not a swimming stroke.
Swimming strokes.Pole vault: Pole vault is a track and field event with a record over 6 meters, not a swimming stroke.
Swimming strokes.Javelin: The javelin is a throwing event in athletics, and it comes from ancient spear throwing.
Swimming strokes.Hurdles: Hurdles are barriers that runners leap in a race, and it is a track event, not a swimming stroke.
Swimming strokes.Cartwheel: A cartwheel is a gymnastic move in which you turn sideways on your hands, so it is not a swimming stroke.
Swimming strokes.Wheelie: A wheelie is lifting a bike's front wheel, so it belongs to cycling rather than swimming.
Swimming strokes.Slalom: Slalom is a skiing race through gates, though there is also a canoe slalom, so it is not swimming.
Swimming strokes.Sprint: Sprint means a short, fast race, and swimmers do sprints, but it is not a stroke itself.

Things with spots.Ladybug: The number of spots doesn't tell a ladybug's age; the bright warning colors tell predators it tastes bad.
Things with spots.Dalmatian: Dalmatian puppies are born pure white, and their spots appear within a few weeks; they were once carriage escorts.
Things with spots.Leopard: Each leopard's rosette pattern is unique, like a fingerprint, and helps it vanish in dappled shade.
Things with spots.Cheetah: Cheetahs have solid black spots, not rosettes, and black tear marks on their faces that cut the sun's glare.
Things with spots.Giraffe: Every giraffe's patch pattern is unique, and the patches help release heat from the animal's blood vessels beneath.
Things with spots.Dice: A standard die has spots called pips, laid out so opposite faces always add up to seven.
Things with spots.Domino: Domino tiles are marked with pips; a double-six set has 28 tiles, and the name may come from a hooded winter cloak.
Things with spots.Fly agaric: The red-capped, white-spotted fly agaric is the classic fairy-tale toadstool, and it is poisonous and hallucinogenic.
Things with spots.Jaguar: Jaguars have rosettes with dots inside, which tell them apart from leopards; they also have the strongest bite of any big cat.
Things with spots.Whale shark: The whale shark is the largest fish in the world, and its spot pattern is unique; scientists use it to identify individuals.
Things with spots.Fawn: Fawns' white spots camouflage them in dappled forest light, and they fade as the deer grows up.
Things with spots.Zebra: A trap: zebras are striped, not spotted, and every zebra's stripe pattern is unique, like a human fingerprint.
Things with spots.Tiger: Tigers are striped, not spotted, and the stripes run into their skin too; a trap if you remember big cats as all spotted.
Things with spots.Robin: The robin's famous red-orange breast has no spots, although young European robins are speckled and lack the red.
Things with spots.Crow: Crows are solid black, not spotted; they're clever enough to recognise human faces and hold grudges.
Things with spots.Polar bear: Polar bears are plain white-looking, with no spots; their hollow guard hairs scatter light to appear white.
Things with spots.Flamingo: Flamingos are pink with no spotting; they get their color from pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat.
Things with spots.Raccoon: Raccoons have a black mask and ringed tail rather than spots; the name 'washing bear' hints at their dunking food.
Things with spots.Lemon: Lemons are plain yellow, with no spots on the skin, and the fruit is an old hybrid of citron and bitter orange.
Things with spots.Swan: Swans are plain white or black, and baby cygnets are grey; no spotted swan exists.
Things with spots.Black cat: A black cat's coat can look faintly striped in bright sun, because the tabby gene is hidden under the black; but no spots.
Things with spots.Panda: Pandas have large black patches, not spots, and the patches make a famous black-and-white look that may help camouflage in snow.
Things with spots.Candy cane: A candy cane is striped red and white, not spotted, and the J shape is often credited to a choirmaster's legend.
Things with spots.Barber pole: A barber pole's stripes come from the old barber-surgeons; red for blood and white for bandages, and it is not spotted.

Ingredients for a witch's potion.Eye of newt: Eye of newt is from Shakespeare's Macbeth; some say it's folk slang for mustard seed, though that's unproven.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Toe of frog: Toe of frog is another Macbeth ingredient, part of the witches' famous cauldron chant 'Double, double toil and trouble'.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Bat wing: Bat wing is a classic witch's ingredient, and in Macbeth the witches add 'wool of bat'.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Dragon scale: Dragon scale is a staple of fantasy potion lore; real-world 'dragon's blood' resin comes from certain palm and tree species.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Unicorn hair: Unicorn hair is a wand core in Harry Potter, and in medieval Europe 'unicorn horn' was often really narwhal tusk.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Mandrake root: Mandrake root really exists and is a toxic plant whose forked roots look vaguely human, which fed myths of it screaming when pulled.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Spider legs: Spider legs are a standard witches' cauldron item in stories; real spider silk is stronger than steel by weight.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Phoenix feather: Phoenix feather is a wand core in Harry Potter, where the bird Fawkes belongs to Dumbledore; the phoenix is a mythical bird.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Snake venom: Snake venom has real medical uses; a drug for high blood pressure was developed from a Brazilian pit viper's venom.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Wolfsbane: Wolfsbane is a real, poisonous plant, also called monkshood or aconite, and was used in legend against werewolves.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Ketchup: A trap: ketchup is a sauce, and with its tomato base it's a pantry item that wouldn't be seen in a witch's brew.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Cornflakes: Cornflakes are a breakfast cereal invented by the Kelloggs in the 1890s, a cauldron nobody would stir.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Peanut butter: Peanut butter is a pantry staple, not a witch's ingredient; it isn't actually made of nuts since peanuts are legumes.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Sprinkles: Sprinkles are a cake decoration, and in Australia they're called hundreds and thousands.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Mayonnaise: Mayonnaise is a mix of egg yolk, oil and acid; it's a kitchen emulsion, not a magic brew.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Cola: Cola was invented in 1886 by pharmacist John Pemberton, and was first sold as a medicine, so it nearly qualifies as a potion.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Ranch dressing: Ranch dressing was invented in the 1950s by Steve Henson at his California dude ranch, and it's no ingredient in a witch's pot.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Chicken nuggets: Chicken nuggets were invented by a Cornell professor, Robert Baker, in the 1960s, and they belong to a kitchen, not a cauldron.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Gummy bears: Gummy bears were invented in Germany in 1922 by Hans Riegel, founder of Haribo; they're sweets, not potion fare.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Cream cheese: Cream cheese is a mild fresh cheese; the first American version came from a New York dairy in 1872.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Maple syrup: Maple syrup takes about 40 litres of sap to make one litre; it's a sweet pantry treat, not a witch's potion ingredient.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Marshmallows: Marshmallows were originally made from the root sap of the marshmallow plant, a herb once used as a remedy.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Instant noodles: Instant noodles were invented in Japan in 1958 by Momofuku Ando; they're quick-cook, not a witch's brew.
Ingredients for a witch's potion.Fish sticks: Fish sticks are breaded fish, a freezer-aisle favourite, and no part of a witch's cauldron.

Jobs ending in '-smith'.Blacksmith: Blacksmiths hammer heated iron, and the name stems from the dark colour of iron, 'black metal'. Smith is among the most common English surnames.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Goldsmith: Goldsmiths worked with gold and were early bankers. London's goldsmiths gave their name to the Goldsmiths' Company, founded in the 1300s.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Silversmith: Silversmiths craft silverware and jewelry. Paul Revere, famous for his midnight ride, was a noted silversmith.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Locksmith: A lock expert. Pin-tumbler locks, still widely used today, are based on a design that goes back thousands of years to ancient Egypt.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Gunsmith: Gunsmiths build and repair firearms. Many American colonial gunsmiths were also frontier craftsmen.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Wordsmith: A person who crafts words skillfully, such as a writer. It's a figurative use of the smith idea, forged in sentences rather than iron.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Tinsmith: Tinsmiths shape tinplate, thin iron coated with tin, into pails and lanterns. In The Wizard of Oz, a tinsmith rebuilt the Tin Woodman's body.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Coppersmith: A craftsperson who shapes copper into kettles, stills and pans. Copper has been worked for roughly 10,000 years.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Swordsmith: A maker of blades. Japanese swordsmiths are celebrated for folding steel repeatedly to create katana with a hard edge.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Playwright: Wright, not smith: from an old word for a maker. A playwright makes plays, as a shipwright makes ships.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Wheelwright: The suffix is 'wright', from Old English for a worker. Wheelwrights built wooden wheels with spokes, rims and iron tires.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Shipwright: A ship builder. Wright means one who shapes, so this -wright job doesn't end in smith.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Cartwright: A cart builder. It's among the common wright surnames, and Ben Cartwright was the family patriarch in Bonanza.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Millwright: A person who builds and maintains mills. Wright again, not smith, and a trade that's still active in factories.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Carpenter: Carpenters work wood. The word comes from Latin for a carriage-maker, but its ending isn't smith.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Cobbler: A shoe repairer. The word also names a baked fruit dessert, since its cobbled-together top looks like cobblestones.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Cooper: Coopers make barrels and casks. The trade is vital for ageing whisky and wine, and survives today.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Tanner: A leather maker who treats hides. Old tanneries used tannin from oak bark, which gave the trade its name.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Mason: A mason works in stone or brick. Freemasons took their name from medieval stonemason guilds.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Potter: A potter shapes clay on a wheel. Harry's last name, Potter, is also one of the most common English job surnames.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Chandler: A candle maker or dealer. Later the word broadened to mean a seller of ship supplies, a 'ship chandler'.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Farrier: A farrier shoes horses. The name comes from Latin 'ferrum', iron, and relates to hooves, not metal smithing alone.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Thatcher: Thatchers make roofs from straw or reed. Margaret Thatcher's surname came from this old craft.
Jobs ending in '-smith'.Weaver: A weaver makes cloth on a loom. The trade gave rise to the Industrial Revolution's famous spinning and weaving machines.

Parts of a ship.Port: Port is the left side of a ship because ships used to tie up on that side at port, while the steering oar was on the right.
Parts of a ship.Starboard: Starboard comes from the Old English for steering side, because early boats were steered with an oar on the right.
Parts of a ship.Bow: The bow is the front of a ship, and it's pronounced to rhyme with cow, unlike the bow of a violin or a bow tie.
Parts of a ship.Stern: The stern is the back of a ship, and the stern of a vessel carried the captain's cabin on old sailing ships, with big windows.
Parts of a ship.Galley: A ship's kitchen is called a galley, and the name comes from the rowing ships that once carried it.
Parts of a ship.Bulkhead: Bulkheads are the walls dividing a ship into watertight compartments, which is why a single breach can't always sink it.
Parts of a ship.Hull: The hull is a ship's main body, and the double-hull design on modern tankers helps prevent oil spills.
Parts of a ship.Deck: The word deck comes from the Dutch for roof or covering, and a ship's decks are numbered from the top down on a liner.
Parts of a ship.Mast: Masts hold sails, and the tallest wooden masts on sailing ships of old were made of tall pines taken from forests, sometimes reserved for the Royal Navy.
Parts of a ship.Keel: The keel is the long beam along the bottom of a ship, and it keeps the vessel stable and stops it from drifting sideways.
Parts of a ship.Helm: The helm is the steering gear, and a helmsman holds the wheel or tiller. Helm comes from the Old English for rudder handle.
Parts of a ship.Bilge: The bilge is the lowest part of the hull where water collects, and the slang bilge, meaning rubbish, comes from it.
Parts of a ship.Crow's nest: The crow's nest is a lookout platform at the top of the mast, and the name may come from the cage in which ships carried crows to find land.
Parts of a ship.Porthole: Portholes are small round windows, and round is stronger than square because stress concentrates in corners, as shown by early jet airliners.
Parts of a ship.Fuselage: The fuselage is an aircraft's main body, from French fuseler, to shape like a spindle, a plane word not a ship one.
Parts of a ship.Tail fin: The tail fin keeps a plane steady in flight, and it's on a plane, not a ship, though ships have a rudder.
Parts of a ship.Runway: A runway is where aircraft take off and land, and numbers are painted on them to match compass headings.
Parts of a ship.Wheel well: Planes tuck their wheels into the wheel well after takeoff, which is not on a ship, whose wheel is the helm.
Parts of a ship.Landing gear: Landing gear takes tremendous force, and must support a plane weighing hundreds of tons when it touches down.
Parts of a ship.Jet engine: Jet engines power airplanes, and some modern ships use gas turbines derived from them, but a typical ship part would be a propeller.
Parts of a ship.Aileron: Ailerons are the hinged parts on the back of wings that make an aircraft roll, and the name is French for little wing.
Parts of a ship.Tarmac: Tarmac is named for tar macadam, a road surface patented in 1902, and now applies to airport ground, not a ship's part.
Parts of a ship.Control tower: The control tower directs aircraft on the ground and in the air, and is part of an airport rather than a ship.
Parts of a ship.Winglet: Winglets are the upturned tips on wings that cut drag and save fuel, a trick from aircraft, not boats.

Jobs that are also verbs.Cook: Cook works as a noun and a verb, and the surname Cook is among the most common English surnames, from the trade.
Jobs that are also verbs.Nurse: Nurse can mean to feed a baby or to care for a wound, so as a verb it is also used for grudges you nurse.
Jobs that are also verbs.Judge: To judge is to form an opinion, and the old saying warns not to judge a book by its cover.
Jobs that are also verbs.Coach: Coach comes from the Hungarian town of Kocs, known for carriages, and later meant a tutor who carries students through exams.
Jobs that are also verbs.Guide: A guide leads, and the verb to guide comes from Old French, and a guidebook's first modern examples were published in the 1800s.
Jobs that are also verbs.Guard: To guard is to protect, and guard is a job in prisons, banks and the royal palace.
Jobs that are also verbs.Pilot: To pilot means to steer or test something, as in a pilot program, a trial run before wider use.
Jobs that are also verbs.Referee: To referee is to oversee a contest, and the word referee also describes scientists who review papers.
Jobs that are also verbs.Usher: To usher means to guide someone, and ushers came from Latin ostium, door, because they were door-keepers.
Jobs that are also verbs.Butcher: To butcher is to botch something, and the job word comes from Old French for a goat slaughterer.
Jobs that are also verbs.Doctor: To doctor means to alter or tamper with something, as in doctoring a photograph, and doctor means teacher in Latin.
Jobs that are also verbs.Tailor: To tailor means to adapt exactly, and tailoring a plan goes back to making a suit to measure.
Jobs that are also verbs.Model: To model is to display clothes, or to make a version of something, as in modeling climate.
Jobs that are also verbs.Vet: Vet is short for veterinarian, and it's also a verb, meaning to check carefully, as in vetting a candidate.
Jobs that are also verbs.Host: To host is to receive guests, and the word comes from the same Latin root as hospital and hotel.
Jobs that are also verbs.Dentist: A dentist is a noun only. Nobody dentists a tooth, and the word comes from French dentiste, from Latin dens, tooth.
Jobs that are also verbs.Surgeon: Surgeon comes from Greek for hand work, and you can't surgeon someone.
Jobs that are also verbs.Lawyer: Lawyer is a noun only. Nobody lawyers a case, though lawyer up is a slang phrase for hiring one.
Jobs that are also verbs.Chef: Chef is French for chief, and you can't chef a meal in formal English.
Jobs that are also verbs.Accountant: Accountant is only a noun, though account is a verb. The job was formalized in Britain in the 1800s with professional bodies.
Jobs that are also verbs.Banker: Banker is only a noun, even though bank works as a verb. The word bank comes from Italian banca, the bench moneylenders used.
Jobs that are also verbs.Pharmacist: Pharmacist is only a noun with no verb form, from the Greek pharmakon, a drug.
Jobs that are also verbs.Librarian: Librarian is only a noun, with no verb. The Library of Alexandria's head was a prestigious post in the ancient world.
Jobs that are also verbs.Florist: Florist is a noun from Latin flos, flower, and there's no verb to florist.

Things a paramedic uses.Stretcher: Modern gurneys fold their legs as they roll into the ambulance, and early stretchers were simply canvas slung between two poles.
Things a paramedic uses.Defibrillator: Automated ones give spoken instructions and shock only if they detect a shockable heart rhythm, so bystanders can use them safely.
Things a paramedic uses.Oxygen mask: Air is only about 21 percent oxygen, and a mask can raise that sharply for a patient who is struggling to breathe.
Things a paramedic uses.Splint: It immobilizes broken bones and eases pain, and in a pinch a splint can be improvised from sticks or rolled newspaper.
Things a paramedic uses.Neck brace: A cervical collar keeps the neck still after a possible spine injury, so movement does not damage the spinal cord further.
Things a paramedic uses.Bandages: Ancient Egyptians used linen strips to bind wounds, and the same cloth was used in the mummification of the dead.
Things a paramedic uses.Blood pressure cuff: Pressure is still measured in millimeters of mercury, a unit left over from the old mercury gauges used in clinics.
Things a paramedic uses.First aid kit: It includes trauma shears with blunt tips, which cut through clothing quickly without cutting into the skin underneath.
Things a paramedic uses.Ambulance: The word comes from the Latin for walking, and the first ambulances were mobile field hospitals in the Napoleonic armies.
Things a paramedic uses.Stethoscope: It lets a paramedic hear breathing and heartbeat even over the noise of the road, which makes it a classic emergency tool.
Things a paramedic uses.Gavel: A mallet that judges and auctioneers bang to command attention, which does nothing for a patient on a roadside.
Things a paramedic uses.Easel: An artist's stand for holding a canvas upright, so it has no job at an accident scene or in an ambulance.
Things a paramedic uses.Whisk: A kitchen tool that whips air into batter, and no medical crew has ever used one to treat an injury.
Things a paramedic uses.Trowel: A small gardening or masonry blade for spreading mortar or digging holes, not for treating anyone who is hurt.
Things a paramedic uses.Pitchfork: A hay-lifting fork with long tines; it is a farmer's tool, and nothing like a stretcher for carrying a patient.
Things a paramedic uses.Lasso: A cowboy's rope loop for catching cattle, which would be a clumsy way to help anyone who needs medical care.
Things a paramedic uses.Sextant: A navigator's tool for measuring angles of the stars, useful at sea but of no help in a roadside emergency.
Things a paramedic uses.Paint roller: A painter's tool, designed to cover walls evenly, so it has no place in an emergency crew's equipment.
Things a paramedic uses.Fishing rod: An angler's rod and line, which a paramedic might see at a lakeside but would never use to treat a patient.
Things a paramedic uses.Anvil: A blacksmith's block that can weigh hundreds of pounds, and a rather heavy thing to carry into an emergency.
Things a paramedic uses.Loom: A weaving frame; the Jacquard loom of 1804 used punched cards, an ancestor of computer programming, but medics have no use for it.
Things a paramedic uses.Rolling pin: A baker's tool for flattening dough into sheets, with no purpose whatever in an ambulance or at an emergency scene.
Things a paramedic uses.Saddle: A rider's seat for horses, which is not a medical seat, though stretchers do get strapped down on wheels.
Things a paramedic uses.Hacksaw: It cuts metal with a fine-toothed blade held under tension, which is not a tool a paramedic would reach for to help a patient.

Things Santa uses at work.Sleigh: The 1823 poem 'A Visit from St. Nicholas' pictured Santa's sleigh pulled by eight named reindeer, shaping the legend we know.
Things Santa uses at work.Reindeer: Both male and female reindeer grow antlers, and males shed theirs in late autumn, so Santa's December team is probably female.
Things Santa uses at work.Naughty list: The idea of a naughty-and-nice list was popularised by the 1934 song 'Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town', which says he knows who's bad or good.
Things Santa uses at work.Nice list: Children write letters to Santa in many countries, and postal services like Canada Post even have a special postcode for replies.
Things Santa uses at work.Sack of toys: Santa's sack is bottomless in the stories; a real one holding presents for every child on Earth would weigh a staggering amount.
Things Santa uses at work.Chimney: In Dutch tradition, Sinterklaas's gifts are left in shoes by the fireplace, an old ancestor of the stocking custom.
Things Santa uses at work.Red suit: Santa wore many colours in older pictures; red won out, helped by Thomas Nast's drawings and later Coca-Cola ads.
Things Santa uses at work.Elves: Santa's elves joined the story in the 1800s, and Clement Moore's poem calls Santa himself 'a right jolly old elf'.
Things Santa uses at work.Workshop: Finland says Santa lives in Korvatunturi in Lapland, and the town of Rovaniemi has a Santa Claus Village on the Arctic Circle.
Things Santa uses at work.Wrapping paper: Gift wrap was a happy accident: in 1917 a Kansas City shop ran out of tissue and the Hall brothers sold fancy envelope liners instead.
Things Santa uses at work.Easter basket: The Easter basket is for the Easter Bunny's egg delivery, a spring tradition rather than a Santa tool.
Things Santa uses at work.Cupid's bow: Cupid's bow and arrows belong to the Roman god of love and Valentine's Day, not to Christmas.
Things Santa uses at work.Leprechaun gold: Leprechaun gold belongs to Irish folklore and St Patrick's Day, with its pot at the end of a rainbow.
Things Santa uses at work.Painted eggs: Painted eggs belong to Easter, symbolising new life; Santa delivers presents, not eggs.
Things Santa uses at work.Surfboard: In Australia, Christmas falls in summer, so Santa sometimes appears on a surfboard, yet it's no standard tool for him.
Things Santa uses at work.Jack-o'-lantern: A jack-o'-lantern is a carved lantern for Halloween, a celebration with roots in Irish tradition.
Things Santa uses at work.Shamrock: The shamrock is Ireland's emblem, tied to Saint Patrick, who is said to have used it to explain the Trinity.
Things Santa uses at work.Pumpkin: Pumpkins are autumn, harvest and Halloween icons, so they belong to October and Thanksgiving rather than Santa's workshop.
Things Santa uses at work.Tooth fairy pillow: The tooth fairy pays kids for lost baby teeth, a separate gift-giver from Santa; the pillow is hers.
Things Santa uses at work.Fireworks: Fireworks light up New Year's Eve, US Independence Day and Diwali, not Santa's quiet midnight delivery.
Things Santa uses at work.Witch's broom: A witch's broom is a Halloween prop; Santa's own flying machine in stories is a reindeer-drawn sleigh.
Things Santa uses at work.Bunny ears: Bunny ears go with the Easter Bunny, whose egg-delivering role reached America through German settlers.
Things Santa uses at work.Beach umbrella: A beach umbrella suits sunbathing, and Santa would only need one on a southern-hemisphere summer Christmas.
Things Santa uses at work.Sunscreen: Sunscreen is a summer product, though in Australia and Brazil Santa's visit lands in peak sun season.

Apple products.iPad: Launched in 2010, the iPad created the modern tablet market and sold millions within months.
Apple products.iMac: The 1998 original came in translucent Bondi blue and helped save Apple from near bankruptcy.
Apple products.MacBook: The MacBook Air famously debuted in 2008 when Steve Jobs pulled it from a manila envelope on stage.
Apple products.iPod: The first iPod, in 2001, promised 1,000 songs in your pocket and helped Apple become a consumer-electronics giant.
Apple products.AirPods: Launched in 2016 alongside the iPhone 7, which dropped the headphone jack, and became one of Apple's best-selling products.
Apple products.Apple Watch: Released in 2015, it has evolved into a health device that can take an ECG and detect falls.
Apple products.Vision Pro: Apple's spatial computer headset, released in 2024, and it launched at $3,499.
Apple products.Mac Mini: The small desktop introduced in 2005 was pitched as a cheap Mac for people bringing their own keyboard and screen.
Apple products.AirTag: Launched in 2021, it uses nearby Apple devices to help locate lost keys, and also can be misused for stalking, so phones warn about it.
Apple products.Apple TV: Apple's streaming box dates back to 2007, and the Apple TV+ service is a separate streaming platform.
Apple products.Galaxy: Samsung's phone line, which began in 2009 and is Apple's biggest rival in phones.
Apple products.Pixel: Google's own phone, launched in 2016, known for its camera software.
Apple products.Kindle: Amazon's e-reader debuted in 2007 and sold out in about five and a half hours.
Apple products.Surface: Microsoft's tablet and laptop line, launched in 2012.
Apple products.Zune: Microsoft's iPod rival, released in 2006 and discontinued by 2012, and it's often remembered for its brown color option.
Apple products.Walkman: Sony's 1979 portable cassette player, and its direct ancestor is the iPod.
Apple products.ThinkPad: Born at IBM in 1992 with the red TrackPoint nub in the keyboard, and now made by Lenovo.
Apple products.Chromebook: A laptop running Google's Chrome OS, popular in schools across the US.
Apple products.Echo Dot: Amazon's puck-shaped smart speaker with Alexa, introduced in 2016 as a small and cheaper Echo.
Apple products.Fitbit: Fitbit was founded in 2007 and bought by Google in 2021.
Apple products.BlackBerry: The phone with a physical keyboard dominated business and was nicknamed the CrackBerry for how addictive its email was.
Apple products.Xbox: Microsoft's game console line, which started in 2001.
Apple products.Roomba: iRobot's robot vacuum, launched in 2002, and the company's engineers previously built military robots.

Brands that have sold laptops.MSI: MSI is a Taiwanese brand known for gaming laptops and graphics cards.
Brands that have sold laptops.Razer: Razer, known for gaming mice, also sells slim Blade laptops that are styled after MacBooks.
Brands that have sold laptops.Microsoft: Microsoft sells Surface laptops, a line begun in 2012 to show off Windows hardware.
Brands that have sold laptops.Samsung: Samsung sells Galaxy Book laptops and also Chromebooks, besides being a big phone maker.
Brands that have sold laptops.Nvidia: Nvidia makes graphics chips for laptops but doesn't sell the laptops under its own name.
Brands that have sold laptops.Logitech: Logitech sells mice, keyboards, and webcams, which are accessories rather than laptops.
Brands that have sold laptops.Seagate: Seagate makes hard drives, which sit inside laptops but aren't laptops themselves.

Brands that have sold laptops.AMD: AMD designs processors that power many laptops, but it doesn't sell the laptops.
Brands that have sold laptops.Bose: Bose is known for headphones and speakers, not laptops.
Brands that have sold laptops.Adobe: Adobe makes software such as Photoshop; it has never sold laptops.

Data structures.Array: It stores items in consecutive memory slots, which is why jumping straight to the thousandth item is instant.
Data structures.Linked list: Each node points to the next one, so inserting in the middle is cheap, but finding the hundredth item means walking past ninety-nine.
Data structures.Stack: Last in, first out, like a pile of plates, and it is what your computer uses to remember where function calls came from.
Data structures.Queue: First in, first out, as in a ticket line, and it keeps print jobs and network packets in order.
Data structures.Hash table: It turns a key into a slot number so lookups are almost instant, and it powers Python dictionaries and JavaScript objects.
Data structures.Tree: Files on your computer sit in one, with folders branching into subfolders, and unlike a real tree, the root is drawn at the top.
Data structures.Graph: Nodes joined by edges can model friendships, roads or the web, and Euler founded the subject by studying the Seven Bridges of Konigsberg.
Data structures.Heap: It keeps the biggest or smallest item on top, which makes it ideal for priority queues, and it is not the same as the memory heap.
Data structures.Set: It holds each item only once, so adding a duplicate does nothing, and it borrows its rules from mathematics.
Data structures.Binary tree: Each node has at most two children, and when kept balanced, searching a million items takes only about twenty steps.
Data structures.Bubble sort: This is a procedure for ordering a list, not a way of storing one, and it is known for being slow.
Data structures.Quicksort: It is an algorithm, not a structure, and Tony Hoare invented it in 1959.
Data structures.Merge sort: It is a method for ordering data, not a container for it, and it was described by von Neumann in 1945.
Data structures.Compiler: It translates source code into a program, so it is a tool, and not a way to organize data.
Data structures.Debugger: It lets developers pause code and inspect it, so it helps with data without being a structure.
Data structures.For loop: This repeats a block of code, so it is a control flow tool, not a way to organize information.
Data structures.Pixel: The word comes from picture element, and one is a unit of an image, not a structure.
Data structures.Firewall: It filters network traffic, and the name borrows from the walls built to stop fires spreading.
Data structures.Router: This hardware forwards packets between networks, and it is a device rather than a way of organizing data.
Data structures.Cookie: It is a small file a website stores in your browser to remember you, and the name comes from the older term magic cookie.
Data structures.Recursion: It is a technique where a function calls itself, and it often walks through trees but is not a structure.
Data structures.Encryption: It scrambles information to keep it private, so it protects data but does not organize it.
Data structures.Interpreter: It runs code line by line instead of translating it all first, and it is a program rather than a structure.
Data structures.Syntax error: This happens when code breaks a language's grammar rules, and it is a mistake, not a data structure.

Famous video game designers.Shigeru Miyamoto: He created Mario, Donkey Kong and Zelda for Nintendo, and Zelda was reportedly inspired by exploring caves and fields as a boy.
Famous video game designers.Hideo Kojima: The Metal Gear creator is a movie lover who once said that his body is about seventy percent made of films.
Famous video game designers.Sid Meier: His name appears on Civilization, Pirates! and Railroad Tycoon, and his famed rule is that a good game is a series of interesting decisions.
Famous video game designers.Will Wright: He designed SimCity and The Sims, and his games are known as sandboxes without win conditions.
Famous video game designers.John Carmack: The programmer behind Doom and Quake pioneered 3D engines, and he later helped found Oculus VR technology.
Famous video game designers.John Romero: He co-created Doom and Quake at id Software and helped popularize deathmatch, a term he coined.
Famous video game designers.Hironobu Sakaguchi: He created Final Fantasy in 1987, reportedly named because he thought it would be his last game before quitting.
Famous video game designers.Toby Fox: He made Undertale mostly by himself in 2015, composing all its music, and it grew into a cult hit.
Famous video game designers.Satoru Iwata: Nintendo's late president was a programmer who worked on Balloon Fight and Kirby, and the Wii and DS came under his leadership.
Famous video game designers.George Lucas: Star Wars made him famous in film, but his company's LucasArts did make classic adventure games like Monkey Island, designed by others.
Famous video game designers.Jim Davis: Garfield's creator is a cartoonist, and his lasagna-loving cat has starred in games, but Davis designed none of them.
Famous video game designers.Walt Disney: Mickey's creator was an animator and theme-park builder, and he died in 1966, a decade before home video games existed.
Famous video game designers.Stan Lee: The Marvel legend co-created Spider-Man and the X-Men in comics, and he only lent his name and cameo to games.
Famous video game designers.Jim Henson: The Muppets puppeteer shaped children's TV, and games with his creations came later from others.
Famous video game designers.Hayao Miyazaki: The Studio Ghibli founder hand-draws animation and has publicly shown doubts about technology, so games are not his field.
Famous video game designers.Tim Burton: He is a gothic film director, and the games based on his films were made by other studios.
Famous video game designers.John Lasseter: A Pixar pioneer who directed Toy Story, he is a film director, and tie-in games were built by others.
Famous video game designers.Matt Groening: The Simpsons creator is a cartoonist, and while many Simpsons games exist, others designed them.
Famous video game designers.Peter Jackson: The Lord of the Rings director made films, not games, though his studio Weta did work on game projects.
Famous video game designers.J.K. Rowling: The Harry Potter author writes novels, and the games from her world were designed by studios.
Famous video game designers.James Cameron: He directed Titanic and Avatar, and his films have game adaptations but he designed none.
Famous video game designers.Ridley Scott: The director of Alien and Gladiator is a filmmaker, and Alien games were made by other developers.
Famous video game designers.Christopher Nolan: The Inception director favors real stunts over computer effects, so he is a filmmaker rather than a game designer.
Famous video game designers.Seth MacFarlane: The Family Guy creator is a comedian, voice actor and singer, but not a game designer.

Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Pong: Atari's 1972 table tennis game was so simple that the company's first prototype machine reportedly jammed from too many coins.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Atari 2600: Launched in 1977, it popularized swappable game cartridges, and the 2600 name is simply its Atari part number, CX2600.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Floppy disk: IBM introduced the 8-inch version in 1971; it held around 80 KB, less than a single modern photo.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Microprocessor: Intel's 4004 of 1971 was the first commercial one, putting a whole computer processor on a single chip the size of a fingernail.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Email: Ray Tomlinson sent the first network message in 1971 and chose the @ symbol to separate user name from computer.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Walkman: Sony's 1979 portable cassette player, whose name was changed for some markets at first, such as Soundabout in the US.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.VHS: JVC launched it in 1976 and won the format war against Sony's Betamax, partly thanks to longer recording times.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Apple I: Steve Wozniak hand-built it in 1976, and it sold for $666.66 as a bare circuit board with no keyboard or case.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Space Invaders: Taito's 1978 arcade hit supposedly caused a coin shortage in Japan, though that tale is more legend than record.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Ethernet: Bob Metcalfe invented it at Xerox PARC in 1973, and the wired networking standard still carries data in offices and homes.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Speak & Spell: Texas Instruments' 1978 toy talked through single-chip speech synthesis, and E.T. used one to phone home.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Apple II: Launched in 1977 with color graphics and open slots, it became one of the first mass-market personal computers.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.iPhone: Apple's 2007 phone arrived about 28 years after the decade's end, so it doesn't fit the 1970s.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.World Wide Web: Tim Berners-Lee proposed it in 1989 and it spread in the early 1990s, long after the 1970s.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Game Boy: Nintendo's handheld came out in 1989 and its brick-like grey case made it nearly indestructible.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Compact disc: The first commercial disc was Billy Joel's 52nd Street in 1982, so the format missed the 1970s.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.NES: Released in Japan in 1983 as the Famicom, it rescued the console market after the 1983 video game crash.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Tetris: Alexey Pajitnov created the block game in Moscow in 1984, a decade after the 1970s ended.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Macintosh: Apple's 1984 computer was introduced in a Super Bowl ad directed by Ridley Scott.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.DVD: The format appeared in 1996 and 1997, far too late for the 1970s.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Windows 95: Released in 1995, it arrived with a launch campaign that used the Rolling Stones song Start Me Up.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Pac-Man: It came out in 1980, just missing the 1970s, and is said to have been inspired by a pizza with a slice missing.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.Commodore 64: Launched in 1982, it's often cited as the best-selling single computer model of all time.
Tech that debuted in the 1970s.MS-DOS: Microsoft's 1981 operating system started as a purchase of 86-DOS for a price reported around 50,000 dollars.

Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Little Mermaid: Andersen's 1837 tale has the heroine trade her voice for legs; in his original she doesn't win the prince and dissolves into sea foam.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Ugly Duckling: Often read as reflecting Andersen's own outsider childhood, it follows a cygnet bullied by farmyard birds until he turns out to be a swan.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Snow Queen: This 1844 tale begins with a shard of a magic mirror lodging in a boy's eye; it inspired Disney's Frozen.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Thumbelina: Her name means 'tiny thumb'; Andersen's 1835 heroine is born from a flower and is no taller than a thumb.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Little Match Girl: Andersen's 1845 story of a freezing child selling matches on New Year's Eve is one of his saddest.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Tin Soldier: A one-legged toy falls for a paper dancer; in Andersen's 1838 tale, they end up melted together in a fire.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Red Shoes: Andersen's 1845 tale of a girl who cannot stop dancing in cursed shoes is among his darkest, with a grim ending.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Nightingale: Set in China, this 1843 story pits a mechanical jeweled bird against a real one that sings to the dying emperor.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Tinderbox: A soldier meets a witch and three dogs with enormous eyes; this 1835 tale was among Andersen's very first stories.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Wild Swans: Eleven brothers are turned into swans, and their sister must knit shirts of stinging nettles to free them.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Fir Tree: Andersen's 1844 melancholy tale follows a tree that longs to grow up, only to be chopped down for Christmas.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Cinderella: Perrault's 1697 French tale, not Andersen's; the Grimms later told their own darker version with a hazel tree.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Hansel and Gretel: Grimm, not Andersen: children abandoned in a forest find a witch's house made of bread and sweets.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Rapunzel: Grimm tale of a girl locked in a tower; her name is the German word for a salad plant, rampion.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Rumpelstiltskin: A Grimm tale of a miller's daughter who must guess a goblin's name to keep her baby, after he spun straw into gold for her.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Snow White: Another Grimm story, not Andersen's, with a poisoned apple and a fairest-of-all mirror; Disney's first feature film was based on it.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Sleeping Beauty: Perrault's 1697 French tale (the Grimms called it Briar Rose); not Andersen's, though Tchaikovsky made it a ballet.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Puss in Boots: A Grimm tale, not Andersen's: in the original, a princess flings the frog against a wall rather than kissing him.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Frog Prince: Another Perrault tale, a cat with boots tricks an ogre into turning into a mouse and eats him; not Andersen's.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Bluebeard: Perrault's French tale of a nobleman with a blue beard and a forbidden room is not by Andersen.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Goldilocks: An English tale first printed by Robert Southey in 1837, where the intruder was an old woman; it's not Andersen's.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.The Golden Goose: A Grimm story about a goose whose golden feathers stick to anyone who touches it; not Andersen's.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Three Little Pigs: An English folktale, not by Andersen: the wolf famously huffs and puffs and blows houses down.
Fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen.Tom Thumb: This tiny hero from English folklore is the size of his father's thumb, and a separate character from Andersen's Thumbelina.

Operas.Carmen: Bizet's 1875 opera flopped at its Paris premiere and its composer died three months later, but its Habanera and Toreador song are now world-famous.
Operas.La Traviata: Verdi's 1853 opera, whose title means "the woman who strayed", was based on a novel by Dumas fils about a Paris courtesan.
Operas.Aida: Verdi's 1871 opera, set in ancient Egypt, premiered in Cairo and is known for its Triumphal March, often staged with live animals.
Operas.Tosca: Puccini's 1900 thriller of passion and political terror in Rome ends with the heroine leaping from the Castel Sant'Angelo.
Operas.La Bohème: Puccini's 1896 tale of poor Parisian artists is the basis for the musical Rent, and its heroine Mimì dies of consumption.
Operas.Madame Butterfly: Puccini's 1904 opera flopped on its first night in Milan, but he revised it and it became one of the most-performed operas today.
Operas.The Magic Flute: Mozart's 1791 comic fairy-tale opera, sung in German, has the Queen of the Night's aria, one of the highest and trickiest in opera.
Operas.Rigoletto: Verdi's 1851 opera about a court jester has the tenor aria La donna è mobile, a tune the composer kept secret before the premiere.
Operas.Turandot: Puccini's last opera, left unfinished at his death in 1924, was completed by another composer, and gives us the aria Nessun dorma.
Operas.Don Giovanni: Mozart's 1787 opera follows the legendary seducer Don Juan, who ends up dragged to hell by a statue of the man he killed.
Operas.Fidelio: Beethoven's only opera, about a wife who disguises herself as a man to rescue her husband from prison, took him ten years and three versions to finish.
Operas.Nabucco: Verdi's 1842 opera about the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar made his name, and its chorus Va, pensiero became an unofficial Italian anthem.
Operas.Otello: Verdi's 1887 opera, based on Shakespeare's Othello, was written when he was in his seventies, long after he'd said he'd retired.
Operas.Swan Lake: Tchaikovsky's 1877 ballet is a ballet, not an opera, and flopped at its premiere before being revived in 1895.
Operas.The Nutcracker: Tchaikovsky's 1892 Christmas ballet came from Hoffmann's story and is danced rather than sung.
Operas.Giselle: The 1841 ballet is a classic of Romantic dance, famous for its ghostly Wilis, and has no singing.
Operas.Coppélia: Delibes's 1870 ballet about a doll who seems alive is a comic dance piece with no opera singers.
Operas.The Firebird: Stravinsky's 1910 score for the Ballets Russes made his name, but it is a ballet, not an opera.
Operas.Bolero: Ravel's 1928 work is a single, relentless, ever-louder crescendo, written for a ballet dancer, and it is not an opera.
Operas.The Four Seasons: Vivaldi's violin concertos paint spring, summer, autumn and winter in music, and they have no singing or story.
Operas.Peter and the Wolf: Prokofiev's 1936 piece is a children's tale narrated over an orchestra, with each character a different instrument, not an opera.
Operas.The Rite of Spring: Stravinsky's 1913 ballet reportedly caused a riot in Paris, but it is dance, not opera.
Operas.Cats: Lloyd Webber's musical, based on T. S. Eliot's poems, is a musical theatre piece rather than an opera.
Operas.Les Misérables: The long-running musical, sung almost throughout, is a musical, not a classical opera, though it is often called operatic.

Novels by H. G. Wells.The Time Machine: Wells's 1895 debut introduced the Eloi and Morlocks, and the term "time machine", for a device you ride through time.
Novels by H. G. Wells.War of the Worlds: Wells's 1898 Martian invasion novel was beaten not by weapons but by Earth's germs; Orson Welles's 1938 radio version caused some alarm.
Novels by H. G. Wells.The Invisible Man: Griffin, a scientist who turns invisible but cannot reverse it, drives this 1897 novel; his clothes remain visible.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Island of Dr. Moreau: A shipwrecked man finds a doctor on a remote island who is turning animals into humanlike beings; the 1896 novel was condemned.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Kipps: His 1905 comic novel about a draper's apprentice who inherits a fortune inspired the musical Half a Sixpence.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Tono-Bungay: A 1909 novel about a patent medicine business, in which Wells paints a picture of Edwardian England.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Ann Veronica: This 1909 novel scandalized readers with a young woman who rebels against her father and chases independence.
Novels by H. G. Wells.The Food of the Gods: A 1904 novel in which a growth formula creates giant wasps, rats and children.
Novels by H. G. Wells.The Sleeper Awakes: A man sleeps for two hundred years in this 1910 novel and wakes to find himself the owner of the world.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Love and Mr Lewisham: A 1900 novel about a young teacher whose ambitions run into love, partly drawn from Wells's own life.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Frankenstein: Mary Shelley's 1818 novel was written when she was 18, and it isn't by Wells.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Dracula: Bram Stoker's 1897 vampire novel was published two years after Wells's debut.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Brave New World: Aldous Huxley's 1932 dystopia comes from a different century of science fiction.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Nineteen Eighty-Four: George Orwell's 1949 dystopia is not by Wells, though Wells's influence is felt.
Novels by H. G. Wells.The Lost World: Arthur Conan Doyle's 1912 dinosaur plateau novel is not Wells's.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Fahrenheit 451: Ray Bradbury's 1953 book-burning novel is a different author's.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Foundation: Isaac Asimov's Foundation stories date from the 1940s; Wells had died by 1946.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Dune: Frank Herbert's 1965 desert-planet epic is not by Wells.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Solaris: Stanisław Lem's 1961 sentient ocean planet isn't Wells.
Novels by H. G. Wells.The Midwich Cuckoos: John Wyndham's 1957 alien-children tale is not by Wells.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Erewhon: Samuel Butler's 1872 satire is not by Wells; its name is "nowhere" backwards.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Flatland: Edwin Abbott's 1884 mathematical satire about two-dimensional beings isn't Wells.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Looking Backward: Edward Bellamy's 1888 utopia about a man waking up in 2000 is American, not Wells.
Novels by H. G. Wells.Treasure Island: Robert Louis Stevenson's 1883 pirate adventure is not by Wells.

Foods traditionally served cold.Gazpacho: Gazpacho is a chilled soup from Andalusia in Spain, and it was traditionally made with bread, tomatoes and olive oil.
Foods traditionally served cold.Potato salad: Potato salad is served cold, and a German version is often made with a warm vinegar dressing, though not the American one.
Foods traditionally served cold.Coleslaw: Coleslaw's name comes from the Dutch 'koolsla', meaning cabbage salad, and it's served chilled.
Foods traditionally served cold.Ceviche: Ceviche is raw fish 'cooked' by the acid in lime juice, and Peru calls it a national dish.
Foods traditionally served cold.Vichyssoise: Vichyssoise is a cold leek and potato soup, and though it sounds French, a chef at the Ritz-Carlton in New York popularized it.
Foods traditionally served cold.Sorbet: Sorbet contains no dairy, and its origins go back centuries to chilled drinks in the Middle East and Persia.
Foods traditionally served cold.Cold brew coffee: Cold brew is steeped for hours in cold water, resulting in a smoother, less acidic coffee.
Foods traditionally served cold.Shrimp cocktail: Shrimp cocktail grew popular in the US in the 20th century, and the 'cocktail' refers to the cold appetizer glass.
Foods traditionally served cold.Panna cotta: Panna cotta means 'cooked cream' in Italian, and it is set with gelatin and chilled until it wobbles.
Foods traditionally served cold.Tiramisu: Tiramisu means 'pick me up' in Italian, and it's a chilled dessert of coffee-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone.
Foods traditionally served cold.Iced tea: Iced tea took off in the US after the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, where a vendor served hot tea over ice.
Foods traditionally served cold.French onion soup: French onion soup is served bubbling hot, with melted cheese over toasted bread.
Foods traditionally served cold.Lasagna: Lasagna is baked and served hot, and it's one of the oldest known pasta dishes.
Foods traditionally served cold.Hot chocolate: Hot chocolate is, by its name, served hot, and the Aztecs drank a bitter, spiced version.
Foods traditionally served cold.Ramen: Ramen is a hot noodle soup, though there is a cold version, hiyashi chuka, served in summer.
Foods traditionally served cold.Cheese fondue: Cheese fondue is kept warm over a flame, and it is a classic Swiss dish.
Foods traditionally served cold.Mashed potatoes: Mashed potatoes are served warm, as cold ones turn gluey and stiff.
Foods traditionally served cold.Chili: Chili is a hot stew, and its fiery taste comes from capsaicin, which triggers heat sensors, not temperature.
Foods traditionally served cold.Pancakes: Pancakes are eaten hot off the griddle, and they go rubbery as they cool.
Foods traditionally served cold.Grilled cheese: A grilled cheese is served hot, so the cheese is melted and the bread is crisp.
Foods traditionally served cold.Baked potato: A baked potato is served hot, and wrapping it in foil actually steams it rather than bakes.
Foods traditionally served cold.Tomato soup: Tomato soup is usually hot, though it has a chilled cousin in gazpacho.
Foods traditionally served cold.Pot pie: A pot pie is baked and served hot, with a flaky crust over a creamy filling.
Foods traditionally served cold.Mac and cheese: Mac and cheese is served hot and gooey, but a cold macaroni salad is a different dish.

Formula One world champions.Lewis Hamilton: He shares the record of seven world titles with Schumacher and holds the all-time record for race wins and poles.
Formula One world champions.Michael Schumacher: The German won five titles in a row with Ferrari from 2000 to 2004, a streak that defined an era.
Formula One world champions.Ayrton Senna: The Brazilian won three titles with McLaren and died in a crash at Imola in 1994, a loss that changed F1 safety.
Formula One world champions.Sebastian Vettel: He became the youngest champion in 2010 at age 23 and won four titles in a row with Red Bull.
Formula One world champions.Max Verstappen: The Dutchman debuted at 17, the youngest F1 driver ever, and won four straight world titles from 2021 to 2024.
Formula One world champions.Fernando Alonso: The Spaniard won back-to-back titles in 2005 and 2006 and was still racing well into his forties.
Formula One world champions.Niki Lauda: The Austrian won the 1976 world title only months after a horrific fire at the Nürburgring, as dramatized in the film Rush.
Formula One world champions.Alain Prost: Nicknamed the Professor, the Frenchman won four titles and had a famous rivalry with Ayrton Senna.
Formula One world champions.Nigel Mansell: The Briton won the 1992 title with Williams, and then moved to America to win the IndyCar championship in 1993.
Formula One world champions.Jenson Button: The British driver won the 2009 title with Brawn GP, a team that had been born from the ashes of Honda only months earlier.
Formula One world champions.Damon Hill: The 1996 champion is the son of Graham Hill, and they are the only father and son to both win the title.
Formula One world champions.Jackie Stewart: The Scot won three titles and became a leading campaigner for racing safety after seeing many friends die.
Formula One world champions.Mario Andretti: The 1978 champion also won the Indianapolis 500 and Daytona 500, and remains one of motor racing's most versatile stars.
Formula One world champions.Stirling Moss: Often called the best driver never to win the title, he finished second in the championship four times.
Formula One world champions.Valentino Rossi: The Italian is a legend of motorcycle racing, with nine world titles, but he never won an F1 championship.
Formula One world champions.Dale Earnhardt: The NASCAR legend won seven Cup titles, but he never raced in Formula One.
Formula One world champions.Jeff Gordon: A four-time NASCAR Cup champion who is not a Formula One champion, and he made his name on American ovals.
Formula One world champions.Danica Patrick: The IndyCar and NASCAR driver led the Indy 500 in 2005, though she never took part in an F1 race.
Formula One world champions.Mark Webber: The Australian won nine Grands Prix but finished third in the 2010 title fight, so he never became champion.
Formula One world champions.Rubens Barrichello: The Brazilian started a record 322 Grands Prix and won 11, but never took a world title.
Formula One world champions.David Coulthard: The Scot won 13 Grands Prix and finished runner-up to Mika Häkkinen in 2001 for the title, but never became champion.
Formula One world champions.Sébastien Loeb: The Frenchman won nine rally world titles in a row, but not an F1 championship.
Formula One world champions.Colin McRae: The Scot was the 1995 World Rally Champion, and his name was given to a famous video game series.
Formula One world champions.Felipe Massa: The Brazilian lost the 2008 title by a single point to Lewis Hamilton on the final corner of the final race.

Fictional drinks.Nuka-Cola: The Fallout series' pre-war cola. Players collect its bottle caps, which serve as currency in the wasteland.
Fictional drinks.Slurm: Futurama's addictive soda is made from the slime of a giant worm queen, and its slogan is "It's highly addictive!"
Fictional drinks.Blue milk: Luke Skywalker drinks this at his aunt and uncle's farm in Star Wars. It's milked from a beast called a bantha.
Fictional drinks.Pumpkin juice: Served in goblets at Hogwarts feasts. Fans make real versions from pumpkin puree and apple juice.
Fictional drinks.Squishee: The frozen slush at The Simpsons' Kwik-E-Mart parodies 7-Eleven's Slurpee. 7-Eleven once converted real stores into Kwik-E-Marts.
Fictional drinks.Buzz Cola: The Simpsons' favorite cola. For the 2007 movie, 7-Eleven briefly sold actual bottles of it.
Fictional drinks.Fizzy lifting drink: In Roald Dahl's Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, it makes you float, but you must burp to get back down.
Fictional drinks.Polyjuice Potion: A Harry Potter brew that makes you look like someone else for an hour. It takes about a month to make and needs a bit of that person.
Fictional drinks.Ent-draught: Tolkien's Entish drink. After sipping it, the hobbits Merry and Pippin grew far taller than any hobbit before.
Fictional drinks.Felix Felicis: Harry Potter's "liquid luck." Ron plays brilliantly after wrongly believing he'd been given some, a sneaky lesson about confidence.
Fictional drinks.Irn-Bru: Real: Scotland's bright orange soda that often rivals Coca-Cola there. Its slogan calls it "made in Scotland from girders."
Fictional drinks.Moxie: Real, and a New England classic with a bitter gentian-root taste. It's Maine's official soft drink.
Fictional drinks.Vimto: A real British soft drink from 1908, and a favorite for breaking the fast during Ramadan in many countries.
Fictional drinks.Tizer: A real British fizzy drink from 1924, long marketed as "The Appetizer," with a distinctive reddish-orange color.
Fictional drinks.Yakult: A real Japanese probiotic drink sold in tiny bottles, built around a bacterium called Lactobacillus casei Shirota.
Fictional drinks.Ribena: A real British blackcurrant cordial. During World War II, it was a key source of vitamin C for children.
Fictional drinks.Kvass: Real, a fermented Eastern European drink made from stale rye bread, usually with very little alcohol.
Fictional drinks.Sarsaparilla: Real, made from the sarsaparilla vine's root. Westerns made it the saloon's non-alcoholic choice, though it began as a medicinal tonic.
Fictional drinks.Orangina: Real, and Peru's bubblegum-flavored golden soda. Coca-Cola bought a stake in the company in 1999.
Fictional drinks.Inca Kola: A real French orange soda with pulp. Its famous instruction is to shake the bottle to mix it.
Fictional drinks.Lilt: Real, a British pineapple-and-grapefruit drink once sold as having a "totally tropical taste."
Fictional drinks.Surge: Real, a citrus soda launched by Coca-Cola in the 1990s. A fan campaign helped bring it back in 2014.
Fictional drinks.Tab: Real. Coca-Cola launched this as its first diet cola in 1963, and it was finally discontinued in 2020.
